searchText: Do we believe that gas refunds are serving their purpose and incentivizing people to clear storage? We have seen that gas refunds are causing *real* problems (gas tokens), so I'm wondering if we should compare the benefits of gas refunds against the costs they are presenting and think about removing/changing them? I think they are NOT serving their intended purpose, but it is quite hard to remove them now, because they are serving other purposes 🙂 unintended ones I don't have a problem breaking gas tokens personally, if that is all they are being used for. <tkstanczak> Gas tokens make this slightly worse than without gas tokens but it is still better than without refunds. Without refunds you do not have incentive for clearing storage at all (unless you introduce some rent as for example in regenesis) I agree with the promise, but do we actually see anyone clearing state because of the gas refunds? Very few contracts I know of go out of their way to clear state for the gas refund with the exception of state they previously added solely so they could later get a gas refund (e.g., gas tokens). <jhancock76> Regenisis seems like a good time to cut ties with gas token tbh That is, I agree with the premise of gas refunds, but unfortunately I don't know that they actually achieved their goals in practice. Personally, I would start with version 4 and then if there was pushback start cutting things, but that is personal preference. Adding multiple versions reduces the number of rounds of communication one has to do to review 🙂 How so? In my experience it just leads to more confusion about "what is state of the art/rough consensus". <jhancock76> Or an informational EIP describing the rational and suggestions. Well, you review all the version, pick the one that makes most sense, or none, and go back to the requestor. Instead of being "fed" one version at a time Difference of "we are doing X unless someone can put forth an argument for something else" vs "we are going to do one of these 5 things, they have all been discussed a lot and there is a secret consensus on what will actually happen but that is opaque to the new reader". I am not arguing it has to make to EIP or not, because I am more relaxed about EIPs, I think people take them too seriously, to be honest 🙂 I am serious about well formed EIPs that can move through the process quickly because of the 204 open pull requests and 432 open issues that are sitting in limbo for one reason or another. 😉 Not to mention the hundreds of Draft EIPs that are stuck because no one is willing to make a decision, or because the author can't seem to trim down their EIP, or because the author included some pork that is getting pushback from some opposition group, etc. > Any way to know which aren’t gas tokens? The data has to be re-collected but should be possible. Mostly I wanted to see what's the ratio of creating new storage slots vs clearing them I'm curious what strategy could be used to identify storage that is created specifically to be cleared. I guess we could start by just looking at well known gas tokens and Chi, though I know that some of the bots follow similar personal strategies that aren't as well publicized. oh, please don't take me too seriously either. But I started to think differently of the EIP process after someone asked me back in January 2019: "how do changes in Ethereum REALLY happen?". And of course, I did not start to describe the EIP process as you can imagine, I tried to explain, what really needs to happen for a change to go through 🙂 My long term goals with the EIP process is to turn it into purely a technical specification process. I have been pushing to get rid of everything related to mainnet inclusion, forking, etc. out of the EIPs process and just have it be a place where people can write very specific/targeted technical specifications. Essentially, it would only be part of the mainnet inclusion process as a side effect of "getting a technical spec drafted is a prerequisite for some other process", not because EIPs are the center of that process. Yes, that would be a correct approach, I think Part of this, IMO, means getting rid of a lot of the debate, history, internal versioning, and even trimming down the motivation/rationale sections quite a bit for a lot of EIPs out there. What really matters is the Specification section, and the other sections are only there to provide useful details for some distant future reader who wants to better understand the EIP. An EIP that just says, "set the gas cost of SSTORE to 500" would be totally valid without needing really much else, since that is sufficient for a technical changeset.
